group.title: Building sentences
group.blurb: The single rule that governs Dutch word order, what happens when you start a sentence with a time or place, and how to turn any statement into a question.

topics.title: Word order and inversion
topics.summary: The verb sits in second position. Always. Everything else in Dutch word order follows from that one fact.

blocks.body:
In a Dutch main clause the **first verb is always the second element**. Not the second word, the second **element**: a whole time phrase or a whole subject counts as one slot.

That gives you two shapes:
- **Standard**: subject first, then the verb.
- **Inversion**: something else first, then the verb, and the subject slides in right after it.

rows: altijd in de zomer naar Frankrijk.
blocks.note: Read the verb column top to bottom. It never moves, whatever happens on the left.

blocks.body:
Inversion is not decoration. Dutch speakers front a word to **highlight** it or to **link** to what was just said.
- `Dit rondje betaal ik.` = This round is on me (not the last one).
- `In december ben ik jarig.` = As for December, that is when my birthday is.
Starting every sentence with the subject is grammatical but flat, so this is one of the quickest ways to sound more fluent.

After the verb and subject, the default order is **Time, Manner, Place**.
- `Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht.` (when, how, where)
- `Wij eten elke zondag samen bij mijn moeder.`
English tends to do the opposite (place before time), which is why `Ik ga naar Utrecht morgen` sounds off to Dutch ears.

sections.heading: The words that do not count as slot one

blocks.title: en, maar, want, dus, of
blocks.body:
These five join two main clauses and stand **outside** the count. The word order after them stays completely normal.
- `Ik loop naar mijn werk **want** het is dichtbij.` (not: want is het dichtbij)
- `Zij komt uit Nederland **en** zij woont in Amsterdam.`
- `Ik wil komen **maar** ik heb geen tijd.`
Compare `dus`, which many people also use with inversion for emphasis: both `dus ik ga naar huis` and `dus ga ik naar huis` are heard.

sections.heading: The second verb goes to the end

blocks.body:
When a sentence has two verbs, only the first one obeys V2. The second stays in its base form and drops to the **end**.
- `Ik wil een biertje **drinken**.`
- `Wij gaan volgend jaar **trouwen**.`
- `Kun je dat **herhalen**?`
Split verbs behave the same way: `Mijn moeder komt vrijdag op bezoek` sends `op` to the end, and `Hoe ziet hij eruit?` sends `eruit` to the end. The **Two verbs in one sentence** sheet works this pattern through in full.

- `geen` sits directly before the noun it cancels: `Ik heb **geen** tijd.`
- `niet` goes to the **end** of the sentence, unless it targets one specific word, in which case it stands just before it: `Ik begrijp de docent **niet**.` versus `Hij is **niet** lang.`

key_takeaways: The first verb is always the second element of a main clause.
Start with anything other than the subject and the subject moves behind the verb.
The rest of the sentence runs Time, Manner, Place.
en, maar, want, dus and of do not count as the first element.
A second verb keeps its base form and goes to the end.

exercises.prompt: Start with In de zomer: we always go to France in the summer.
exercises.explain: The time phrase fills slot one, so the verb comes next and we slides in behind it.

exercises.prompt: Start with In december: my birthday is in December.
exercises.explain: Inversion: the verb ben stays in second position and ik follows it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence puts the verb in the right place after Vrijdag?
options: Vrijdag mijn moeder komt op bezoek.
Vrijdag komt mijn moeder op bezoek.
Vrijdag komt op bezoek mijn moeder.
Komt vrijdag mijn moeder op bezoek.
exercises.explain: Vrijdag is the first element, so the verb must be second and the subject follows it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence keeps the right word order after want?
options: Ik loop naar mijn werk want is het dichtbij.
Ik loop naar mijn werk want het is dichtbij.
Ik loop naar mijn werk, want dichtbij het is.
Ik loop want naar mijn werk het is dichtbij.
exercises.explain: want does not count as an element, so the clause after it keeps normal subject-verb order.

exercises.prompt: Build: I am going to Utrecht by train tomorrow.
exercises.explain: Time (morgen), manner (met de trein), place (naar Utrecht).

exercises.prompt: Start with Dit rondje: I am paying for this round.
exercises.explain: Fronting the object puts the emphasis on it, and the subject moves behind the verb.

exercises.prompt: Build: we want to drink a beer.
exercises.explain: The first verb keeps position two, the second verb drops to the end in its base form.

exercises.prompt: Which is the most natural Dutch order?
exercises.explain: Time comes before place in Dutch, and the subject stays in slot one here.

topics.title: Asking questions
topics.summary: Two question types, one shared shape. Move the verb to the front for yes/no, put a question word before it for everything else.

blocks.body:
Take the statement and put the **verb first**. Nothing else changes.
- `Hij spreekt tien talen.` gives `Spreekt hij tien talen?`
- `Wij leren Nederlands.` gives `Leren wij Nederlands?`
- `Zij woont in Utrecht.` gives `Woont zij in Utrecht?`

blocks.title: With jij or je the -t disappears
blocks.body:
- `Jij bent docent.` gives `**Ben** je docent?` (not bent je)
- `Jij kookt pasta.` gives `**Kook** jij pasta?`
- `Jij hebt tijd.` gives `**Heb** je tijd?`
With `u`, `hij` or a plural the t stays: `Bent u docent?`, `Kookt hij pasta?`, `Koken jullie pasta?`

items.note: hoor softens the answer, it means nothing on its own

items.en: Yes it is! (contradicting a negative question)

blocks.title: The shape
blocks.body:
`Question word + verb + subject + rest`
- `Waarom leer je Nederlands?`
- `Hoeveel broers heb je?`
- `Welke boeken heeft jouw moeder?`
It is the same inversion as before: the question word is the first element, so the verb has to be second.

Same logic as the adjective ending.
- `welk` before a **singular het-word**: `welk land`, `welk boek`, `welk huis`
- `welke` everywhere else: `welke stad`, `welke talen`, `welke kleur`

items.en: What colour eyes does he have?

sections.heading: When the question word IS the subject

blocks.body:
Compare these three:
1. `Is deze plaats vrij?` (yes/no: verb first)
2. `Welke dag is het vandaag?` (question word, then verb, then subject `het`)
3. `Wie is jonger, hij of jij?` (question word `wie` **is** the subject, so nothing inverts)

When `wie` or `wat` is doing the action, there is no separate subject to move: `Wie komt er vanavond?`, `Wat gebeurt er?`

Some question phrases break in two, with the second half going to the end of the sentence.
- `Waar kom je **vandaan**?` (where from)
- `Waar ga je **naartoe**?` (where to)
- `Waar praten jullie **over**?` (what about)
The pattern is `waar` plus a preposition, and the preposition lands at the end.

items.nl: Weet u misschien hoe laat het is?
items.en: Do you perhaps know what time it is?

items.nl: Sorry, mag ik u iets vragen?
items.en: Sorry, may I ask you something?

blocks.title: misschien and even soften everything
blocks.body: Dropping `misschien` (perhaps) or `even` (just briefly) into a request makes it sound much less blunt: `Heb je even tijd?`, `Weet u misschien waar het station is?`

key_takeaways: Yes/no question: verb first, and drop the -t before jij or je.
Question word plus verb plus subject plus rest.
welk before a singular het-word, welke everywhere else.
If wie or wat is the subject, nothing inverts: Wie komt er?
waar plus a preposition splits, and the preposition goes to the end.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: hoe / heten / jouw / kinderen
exercises.explain: Question word, verb, then the subject jouw kinderen. Plural subject takes the base form heten.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: wonen / ouders / waar / jouw
exercises.explain: waar plus the verb plus the subject jouw ouders.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: zus / jouw / welke / spreekt / talen
exercises.explain: welke stays glued to its noun talen, and together they form the first element.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: je / hoeveel / ooms / tantes / heb / en
exercises.explain: hoeveel plus the nouns is the first element. hebt loses its t before je.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: ben / waarom / je / moe
exercises.explain: waarom, then the verb, then the subject. bent loses its t before je.

exercises.prompt: Turn 'Jij kookt pasta' into a question.
exercises.explain: The verb moves to the front and jij right after it removes the -t.

exercises.prompt: Turn 'Hij spreekt tien talen' into a question.
exercises.explain: The -t only drops for jij and je. hij keeps it.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Uit ___ land kom je?
exercises.explain: het land is a singular het-word, so welk with no -e.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Uit ___ stad kom je?
exercises.explain: de stad is a de-word, so welke.

exercises.prompt: Which question needs NO inversion?
options: Wie is jonger, hij of jij?
exercises.explain: wie is the subject here, so there is no other subject to move behind the verb.

exercises.prompt: Build: where are you going to?
exercises.explain: waar plus naartoe splits, and naartoe lands at the end.

topics.title: Two verbs in one sentence
topics.summary: The first verb stays in second position and the second one drops to the very end, unchanged. This one pattern unlocks wanting, having to, being able to, and every plan you make.

blocks.body:
Only the **first** verb obeys the V2 rule and gets conjugated. The **second** verb goes to the **end of the sentence** and stays in its base form (the dictionary form).

`subject + verb 1 + everything else + verb 2`

blocks.note: Everything piles up in the middle. The longer the sentence, the further apart the two verbs sit, which is what makes Dutch feel back-loaded to English speakers.

blocks.title: Do not conjugate the second verb
blocks.body: It is `Ik wil een biertje **drinken**`, never `Ik wil een biertje drinkt`. The second verb never changes, whoever the subject is.

blocks.title: The four you will use most, conjugated
blocks.note: These are irregular in the singular, so the ik and hij forms have no -t. In a question with je the t drops as usual: kun je, wil je, moet je, mag je.

blocks.body:
If the missing verb is obvious, Dutch simply leaves it out. This happens almost always with movement.
- `Zullen we naar de bioscoop?` (gaan is understood)
- `Ik moet naar huis.` (gaan is understood)
- `Ik wil een koffie.` (hebben or drinken is understood)
Both versions are correct. The short one sounds more natural in speech.

sections.heading: om ... te plus the base form

blocks.body:
To say **in order to**, or after a noun or adjective that needs a verb, Dutch uses `om` plus `te` plus the base form. The `te` and the verb sit together at the end.
- `Heb je zin **om** morgen **te zwemmen**?`
- `Ik heb geen tijd **om te koken**.`
- `Ik ga naar de markt **om** groente **te kopen**.`
- `Het is te laat **om** nog **te bellen**.`

blocks.title: Not after the modal verbs
blocks.body: Never combine the two patterns. It is `Ik wil koken`, never `Ik wil om te koken`. `om ... te` only appears after nouns, adjectives, and purpose, not after willen, kunnen, moeten, mogen, zullen or gaan.

A verb like `opbellen`, `meegaan`, `aankomen` or `afrekenen` splits when it is the **conjugated** verb, but stays whole when it is the **second** verb at the end.
- `Ik **bel** je morgen **op**.` (conjugated, so it splits)
- `Ik wil je morgen **opbellen**.` (second verb, so it stays whole)
- `**Ga** je **mee**?` versus `Wil je **meegaan**?`

items.nl: Ik reken bij de bar af.
De trein komt om negen uur aan.

key_takeaways: Verb 1 is conjugated and sits in second position, verb 2 goes to the end in its base form.
willen, kunnen, moeten, mogen, zullen, gaan, komen, blijven and laten all start the pattern.
kan, wil, moet and mag take no -t in the ik and hij forms.
Drop the second verb when it is obvious: Zullen we naar de bioscoop?
om ... te goes with nouns, adjectives and purpose, never after a modal verb.

exercises.prompt: Build: I want to drink a beer.
exercises.explain: wil takes second position, drinken drops to the end in its base form.

exercises.prompt: Build: we are getting married next year.
exercises.explain: The time phrase sits in the middle, between the two verbs.

exercises.prompt: Which two-verb sentence is correct?
options: Ik wil om een biertje te drinken.
exercises.explain: The second verb keeps its base form and goes to the end. om ... te never follows a modal verb.

exercises.prompt: Complete with kunnen: ___ je mij helpen?
exercises.explain: kunt loses its t before je, giving kun je. kan je is also heard.

exercises.prompt: Build: do you feel like swimming tomorrow?
exercises.explain: zin hebben is followed by om ... te, and te plus the verb close the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence combines willen and koken correctly?
exercises.explain: After a modal verb the base form stands alone, with no om and no te.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence handles the split verb opbellen correctly?
options: Ik wil je morgen bel op.
exercises.explain: As the second verb it stays whole at the end. It only splits when it is the conjugated verb: Ik bel je morgen op.

exercises.prompt: Complete the split verb: Ik ___ je morgen op. (opbellen)
exercises.explain: The conjugated part comes second and the prefix op goes to the end.

exercises.prompt: Zullen we naar de bioscoop? What happened to the second verb?
options: it was forgotten, the sentence is wrong
gaan is left out because it is obvious
exercises.explain: With movement the infinitive is usually dropped. Zullen we naar de bioscoop gaan? is equally correct.
